title: CLAY CITY SCHOOL BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay City School Board met Tuesday evening, a week earlier than usual, so they could get ready for the upcoming tax levy process.

Board Chair Misty Lindeman called the meeting to order and asked members to approve the agenda and past minutes. They did so unanimously.

Superintendent John Newbaum then unfurled a banner that will hang in the hallway. It recognizes Clay City Elementary for earning an Exemplary rating. Lindeman congratulated the elementary teachers for a job well done. The teachers who attended stepped forward, and everyone posed for a photo. Lindeman thanked them again and noted how far the students and school have come.

Newbaum moved on to the financial report. He said most fund accounts look solid, though diesel fuel and electricity costs remain high. He plans to talk with a consulting firm about possible electricity savings. The district already has a low rate, but capacity charges push the total cost up. Food prices are also a concern, so the district is looking at joining a new food cooperative to help bring those costs down. The board approved the financial report without dissent.

On the school report card, Newbaum said the overall results were good. The elementary school earned that Exemplary rating, while the junior high and high school both received Commendable ratings.

Principal Brian Wattles presented his report.  He notes that Pre-K kicked off the month with a fun trip to Strief’s Pumpkin Patch.  Kindergarten is wrapping up letter names and sounds and is learning basic 2D shapes while making shape turkeys.  Second graders jumped into the engineering process in science asking questions, imagining solutions and planning, creating, and improving their designs.  Third graders are tackling multiplication and are ready to start their Macy’s Day Parade project and host a balloon parade next week.  Fourth graders are working on their goal of passing 100 i-Ready lessons and hope to celebrate with a gingerbread house decorating contest. They also finished learning about the five regions of the United States, choosing the Southeast and will make jambalaya together.  Fourth and fifth graders art classes plan to put on an art show by the end of the school year to show off their work.  High school students enjoyed field trips to Willard Library and an Evansville Thunderbolts hockey game while FFA members attended the National Convention.  Student Council ran Red Ribbon Week with dress-up days and donated books to the elementary classrooms and hosted a second successful Blood Drive. Mrs. Goodrum brought in author Marc Tyler Nobleman for a visit. Mrs. Hildebrand’s Civics class visited the polls on Election Day, and two students—Jackson Dye and Jalyn Winchester—served as Student Election Judges.  CCHS celebrated Homecoming Week with dress-up days and class wars, then wrapped it up with the Homecoming dance. Congratulations to King Jackson Dye and Queen Taylee Gray!  The junior class also hosted a Father/Daughter Dance that drew a solid turnout.

In new business, the board discussed the tentative tax levy for fiscal year 2027. Newbaum explained that the district has under taxed for a long time, compared with its actual needs.  He says a simple 4.99 percent increase is not sufficient for district needs. Lindeman and Newbaum both know how complicated it is to understand how these changes affect individual taxpayers and stress that this percentage is not the increase people will see on their property tax bills. The actual change depends on each property’s assessed value. As an example, a $100,000 home would see roughly a $30 increase for the year and a home valued at $200,000 would see about a $60 increase. With that information in mind, the anticipated EAV (Equalized Assessed Valuation) is expected to be 10.5 percent.  The district is looking at a 14.84 percent increase in the tax levy itself. That money would support the recently authorized and added responsibility of paying for the school resource officer, along with the needed funds for operations and maintenance and for the transportation fund.  The district has scheduled a Truth in Taxation hearing for December 17 at 6 p.m. prior to the next regular board meeting so the public can ask questions and share concerns.

The board also unanimously approved an update to its policy that switches from dated coverage to rolling coverage for FMLA leave. They added the school resource officer’s salary to the risk management plan because the position is tied to student safety.

Finally, members heard a sample reading of a non-binding ballot question that will appear in the April election. The question simply asks whether voters in the Clay City School District would consider deactivating Clay City High School. It is not a binding decision, it’s more of a way to gauge the public’s opinion.

title: CCHD DENTAL GRANT
full_story:
The Clay County Health Department is expanding its dental services after receiving a 20-thousand-dollar Community Grant from Delta Dental of Illinois Foundation.

This marks the third time the department has received the grant, bringing its total funding to 37,000 since the Oral Health Program launched in 2024.  Over the past two years, the program has handed out more than 3,000 oral health kits and provided exams, cleanings, and fluoride treatments to over 150 adults through its mobile clinics.

Officials say the new funding, combined with a previous grant, will allow the department to add dental x-ray services and begin treating children, including those covered by Youth Care insurance.  Public Health Educator April Carruthers called the expansion a “game changer” for the area, noting that adding local x-rays will reduce travel times for patients in a dental desert.

To qualify for the adult clinics, residents must live in Clay County or receive WIC services through the department, be at least 20 years old, meet income guidelines, have Medicaid or no insurance, and have not seen a dentist in the past year.

Anyone with questions or looking to join the waitlist for the adult or child dental clinics can call April at 618-662-4406.

title: NOMINATION FORMS
full_story:
The Flora Chamber of Commerce has opened the nomination period for Business of the year, New Business of the Year, Citizen of the year and Non-Profit organization of the year.

The Chamber Banquet will take place on January 30th and will honor the winning entries.  The Chamber wants people to take time to read the criteria for nomination for all three entries. You also don’t have to nominate someone for each category, but the Chamber would like to have a short essay on why you are nominating that person, non-profit, new business or business of the year.

Nomination forms can be accessed through the Chamber’s Website or follow the link on the Chamber’s Facebook page.

The deadline to submit nomination is Monday, December 7th. Forms can be emailed to [email protected], mailed to the Chamber office at 223 West Railroad Street or drop it off at the chamber office.

title: CAR DEER ACCIDENT
full_story:
Two people are recovering following a single-vehicle rollover crash near Iuka Sunday night.

According to the Marion County Sheriff’s Department, the crash happened around 9:30 Sunday evening in the 2900 block of Iuka Road.  Investigators say 18-year-old Ashton Hodge of Iuka swerved to avoid hitting a deer.  His vehicle went out of control, overturned once, and landed upright in a roadside ditch.

Hodge was taken to Salem Township Hospital for treatment.  Three passengers were also in the car, 19-year-old Cheyenne Neff and 18-year-old Aiden Doolen, both of Iuka, along with 18-year-old Izaic Bechtel of Alma.

United Medical Response evaluated all three passengers at the scene, and one was also transported to Salem Township Hospital.  The Iuka Fire Department assisted at the crash site.

title: IMAGINATION LIBRARY COMING
full_story:
The Regional Office of Education #12 announced that it is partnering with local program partners in three counties to bring Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library to those areas.

The Imagination Library is a program created by the late singer-songwriter dedicated to inspiring the love of reading by gifting books free of charge to children from birth to age five.

The ROE #12 will be working with the Clay County Community Health Foundation to help establish the program in Clay County.

Also participating is the Friends of the Library of the Lawrence Public Library District in Lawrence County, and the East Richland County Foundation for Academic Excellence (ERCFAE).

For additional information and updates about Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, visit the website: https://roe12.org/.

title: HUNT SMART CLIMB SAFE
full_story:
As hunters across Illinois prepare for the upcoming firearm deer season November 20-22 and December 3-6, the Illinois Department of Natural Resources (IDNR) urges them to use safety harnesses when hunting from tree stands in the field.  Falls from tree stands and elevated blinds are the No. 1 source of hunting-related accidents and fatalities in Illinois.

In 2025, more than half of all hunting incidents reported to IDNR involved tree stands, including failure to use a fall arrest system.

So far during the fall 2026 hunting season, conservation police have documented six serious tree stand falls, two of which involved fatalities.  Of the cases resulting in serious injuries, one hunter fell 25 feet from a saddle stand when he was unable to properly lock it into place.  Another fell to the ground and suffered a broken leg when his tree stand cables snapped.  A third hunter suffered an apparent spinal injury and broken ribs when the strap holding his stand’s platform to the tree snapped.  Another hunter fell about 12 feet when he stood up to shoot a deer and his foot got tangled in the stand.

“Above all else, conservation police want every hunter to make it home safely after each outing,” said Jed Whitchurch, director of IDNR’s Office of Law Enforcement.  “While we encourage hunters to enjoy their time outdoors and achieve their goals, staying alert and prioritizing safety is essential.  A great hunt starts and ends with smart choices.”

Tree stand falls, often from heights of 20 to 30 feet, can cause significant injuries, including broken bones, spinal damage, paralysis, concussions, organ injuries, internal bleeding, sprains, cuts, and bruises.  Most of these injuries are preventable by using fall arrest systems, avoiding drug and alcohol use, and making sure the tree stand equipment is in good working order.

“Tree stand injuries are largely preventable when hunters use reliable fall arrest gear and inspect every part of their stand before climbing,” Whitchurch said.  “The thrill of the hunt should never come at the cost of your health, and that is why conservation police urge hunters to make safety their first step, every single time.”

There were 10 tree stand-related falls in 2025, 15 in 2024, one of which was fatal, 17, in 2023, three of which were fatal, 6 in 2022 and 13 in 2021.

For more information about hunting safety, visit IDNR’s hunter safety website.

title: OPERATION CHRISTMAS CHILD
full_story:
Nearly 5,000 drop-off locations for Operation Christmas Child are now open.

Volunteers across the country are preparing to collect shoeboxes for this year’s Operation Christmas Child, one of the projects of Samaritan’s Purse.  Over the last 33 years, the project has collected and delivered shoeboxes filled with toys, school supplies, and personal care items to millions of children around the world.  Many of those children are suffering from war, poverty, disease and disaster.

For those who wish to participate in this year’s project, you can find a step-by-step guide on the How to Pack a Shoebox the link in this story Operation Christmas Child.  The project partners with different churches across the world to deliver the boxes once they’ve been collected. You can also donate $10 per shoebox gift online through “Follow Your Box” to receive a tracking label and discover its destination.

“Shoebox gifts may seem simple, but they have an eternal impact.  Each box is an opportunity to tell a boy or girl in need about the true meaning of Christmas,” said Franklin Graham, president of Samaritan’s Purse.  “I’ve delivered these boxes around the world, and I never get tired of seeing the joy that they bring, even in the midst of disasters, war, and poverty.”

Operation Christmas Child has collected and delivered more than 244 million gift-filled shoeboxes and delivered them to children in more than 175 countries and territories.

Collection week continues through Monday.  In Flora the drop off location is Christ’s Church, packages will be collected today from 1 to 3 pm, tomorrow from 9 to 11am, Friday, from 1 to 3 pm and from 5 to 7 pm, on Saturday, from 10 to Noon, on Sunday, from 9:30 am to 1:30 pm and on Monday, from 7 to 9 am.

title: 32 STATES OPT IN
full_story:
Governor JB Pritzker can prioritize Illinois students by joining a majority of states and opting into a federal program to provide money for access to needed educational support.

With the potential to unlock as much as $1 billion for Illinois students’ targeted needs, the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program allows public and private school students to receive donor-funded assistance for tutoring, college admission test preparation, special-needs services and more.

Most recently, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she intends to opt her state into the program as she is “supportive of the federal tax credit scholarship and its potential to help New York students and schools.”

Colorado Governor Jared Polis plans to opt his state into program, calling it a no-brainer.

“The more Democratic governors learn about it, I fully expect that most will come around and participate,” Polis said.  “Because from our perspective, it’s free money.”

Along with New York and Colorado, the other Democrat-led states planning to opt in are Kansas, Kentucky and North Carolina.

Jorge Elorza, CEO of Democrats for Education Reform, has said that “if a state does not opt in, then by default, the first $1,700 in every single federal taxpayer’s taxes is going to leave your state.”  Referring to polling, Elorza said that “opting in is not just popular, it is overwhelmingly popular.”

In a nonbinding ballot question in 31 counties in the March 17th primary, 63% of those who voted on the measure supported participating in the program.  Also, 12 county boards in Illinois have adopted resolutions urging Pritzker to opt in.

Pritzker must decide by January 1st, whether to opt Illinois into the program.
